newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Gold prices moved little by U.S. strike on Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Gold prices moved little by U.S. strike on Iraq.

text.p: Despite a small rally in gold prices on news of U.S. missile strikes on Iraq on Tuesday, Asian dealers did not think bullion had much more upside, or scope to recover its traditional role as a haven for funds in a crisis.
"Market sentiment is still unsure and people are sceptical," one dealer at a Hong Kong bank said. "I think people would prefer to see gold higher before buying."

Spot gold in the Hong Kong market firmed minutes after the United States launched its missile strikes and was quoted at US$387.20/387.50 an ounce at 2.30 p.m. local time (0630 GMT), up from $386.70/387.20 an ounce at noon.
Hong Kong dealers said they expected gold to firm to $388.00/388.50 an ounce but to remain range-bound at those levels.
Spot gold prices in Tokyo also rose slightly on Tuesday, reaching $387.10/387.60 an ounce immediately after the news of the U.S. missile strikes, up from $386.65/387.15 in London on Monday.
Japanese traders said the Tokyo market's reaction to the missile attacks was minimal and that they were waiting to see how the London and New York bullion markets responded.
They said that without any further escalation of U.S.-Iraq tensions, the market was unlikely to score additional gains.
"We're only getting one tick per missile," said a source at a leading Japanese trade house. "President Clinton probably isn't hoping for a prolonged conflict," he added.
An analyst for a commodity broker echoed this view. "If there are additional attacks, the gold price may rise further," he said, but otherwise gold's upside appeared limited.

"People are a little bit nervous," said Anderson Cheung, chief dealer at Swiss Bank Corporation's Hong Kong office. But he said that while gold had picked up a little, he did not expect any major moves.
The U.S. military launched cruise missile strikes against air defense targets in Iraq in retaliation for Iraqi military attacks against Kurds in the north, the Pentagon said.
When Iraqi troops invaded Kuwait on August 1, 1990 after a long-running dispute over border oilfields, the gold price jumped nearly $20 to a fix of $382.00 the following day.
The metal then hit a peak of $415.70 on August 23 before slipping back.
On the eve of the allied invasion to remove occupying Iraqi troops, gold had climbed again to fix at $403.70 in London.
The offensive began in the early hours of January 17, 1991 provoking a huge sell-off of gold, which fixed at $383.50 at 1030 GMT in London that day.
